summary: Anaphylaxis under general anesthesia looks different from the ED presentation — the classic symptoms (itching, throat tightness, a sense of doom) are invisible in a sedated, paralyzed, draped patient, so hypotension and bronchospasm are often the ONLY clues. The cause distribution is also different from the general population (NMBAs lead, not food/insect stings), and the diagnostic workup afterward (tryptase timing, allergy referral) is genuinely OR-specific.
whyThisMatters: A patient under general anesthesia cannot tell you they're itchy or that their throat feels tight — the usual first symptoms of anaphylaxis that prompt recognition everywhere else are simply unavailable, so unexplained hypotension or a sudden rise in airway pressure/bronchospasm after a new drug exposure has to BE the trigger for considering anaphylaxis, not a late confirmatory finding.
clinicalTakeaway:
In the OR, treat unexplained hypotension and/or bronchospasm shortly after a new drug/agent exposure as anaphylaxis until proven otherwise — epinephrine is still first-line treatment, same as anywhere else.

Think NMBAs, antibiotics, chlorhexidine, and sugammadex first when reviewing what the patient was exposed to (not the food/insect-sting causes that dominate outside the OR).

After stabilization, draw:
- an acute tryptase within 30 minutes-2 hours of onset
- AND a baseline tryptase at least 24 hours after full resolution

A single tryptase level without a baseline for comparison is much less useful, since baseline levels vary between individuals.

body.text: Why it presents differently under anesthesia

The patient is:
- sedated (can't report itching, throat tightness, or a sense of impending doom)
- paralyzed (can't develop visible stridor/respiratory distress the way an awake patient would)
- draped (skin flushing/urticaria may not be visible or may be the LAST thing noticed rather than the first)

This means the presentation is dominated by objective hemodynamic and respiratory findings: sudden, otherwise-unexplained hypotension (sometimes severe/refractory) and/or a sudden rise in peak airway pressure or new bronchospasm.

Either — or both — after a new drug exposure should trigger consideration of anaphylaxis.
Cause distribution — different from the general population

Other (latex, sugammadex, opioids, colloids, protamine, and others)

body.text: Sugammadex is an increasingly recognized cause of perioperative anaphylaxis in its own right — not merely a marker of underlying rocuronium allergy. As sugammadex use has expanded, reports of anaphylaxis specifically to sugammadex itself have grown; consider it on the differential when reaction timing lines up with reversal rather than induction.

items: Chlorhexidine deserves specific attention because it's everywhere in the perioperative environment (skin prep, central line kits, some coated catheters, some lubricants) and easy to overlook as a cause since it isn't a 'drug' in the way NMBAs and antibiotics are.

Latex remains a cause, though its relative share has declined over recent decades with reduced latex use in many ORs — still worth asking about in a patient with a documented latex allergy or spina bifida (a recognized latex-sensitization risk group).

Review the full timeline of everything the patient was exposed to — induction agents, NMBA, antibiotics, skin prep, any dyes, colloid volume expanders, protamine (if used) — rather than assuming it must be the most recently given drug.

body.text: The core treatment algorithm is IDENTICAL to anaphylaxis anywhere else — epinephrine first-line (IV titrated boluses or an infusion are typical in the OR setting given IV access is already established, rather than IM as in the ED/prehospital setting), stop the presumed triggering agent, fluid resuscitation for hypotension, and secure/support the airway as needed — see the main anaphylaxis reference for the full algorithm, which this module doesn't restate.
Tryptase — timing is everything for a useful result

items: Acute (event) tryptase: draw within roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours after symptom onset — tryptase peaks quickly (often within an hour) and has a half-life of only 1.5-2.5 hours, so a level drawn too late can already be falling back toward baseline and understate the true peak.

Baseline (convalescent) tryptase: draw at least 24 hours after all symptoms have FULLY resolved (or use a pre-existing pre-op sample if available) — this is essential for interpretation, since baseline tryptase varies meaningfully between individuals, and a single acute-only level can't distinguish 'elevated for this patient' from 'this patient normally runs high.'
Interpretation: an acute level exceeding roughly [2 + (1.2 × baseline)] supports genuine mast-cell activation — a rise-from-baseline calculation, not a fixed absolute cutoff.

Refer to an allergist/immunologist for formal testing (skin testing, specific IgE where available) once the patient has recovered — identifying the actual culprit agent matters enormously for future anesthetic planning, and empiric avoidance of an entire drug class without confirmed testing can unnecessarily limit future anesthetic options.

buildNote: Deliberately does not restate the core epinephrine-dosing/anaphylaxis-treatment algorithm, which is identical to the existing anaphylaxis module — this module's value is entirely in what's DIFFERENT about the OR context: presentation, cause distribution, and the tryptase-timing workup.
